### E.5 Consistency Heads Patching

Figure [18](#A6.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It")
shows the models’ accuracy in detecting consistent errors at both the
position of the arithmetic result and the final numeric answer, before
and after patching a small subset of *consistency* heads, as outlined in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Dissociation of Arithmetic Validation and Computation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It").
For the exact list of patched heads, please refer to
Table [4](#A4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix D Experiment Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It").
Consistent with the results reported in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Dissociation of Arithmetic Validation and Computation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It")
for Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct, we observe a significant improvement in
accuracy for Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and
Phi-3-Mini-4k-Instruct.

### E.6 Computation Circuits

As outlined in
Section [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Circuits for Arithmetic Computation ‣ Appendix D Experiment Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It"),
we identify the circuits responsible for predicting the correct
arithmetic result of the equations in the prompts described in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Circuits for Arithmetic Error Detection ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It").
Table [12](#A6.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It")

models and templates. Results for the faithfulness scores and sizes of
the *soft intersection circuits* $`\mathcal{C}^{(\tau)}`$ for different
threshold values $`\tau`$ for all models are shown in
Figures [10(c)](#A6.F10.sf3 "Figure 10(c) ‣ Figure 10 ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It"),
[11(c)](#A6.F11.sf3 "Figure 11(c) ‣ Figure 11 ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It"),
[12(c)](#A6.F12.sf3 "Figure 12(c) ‣ Figure 12 ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It"),
and
[13(c)](#A6.F13.sf3 "Figure 13(c) ‣ Figure 13 ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It"),
respectively. The final circuits are visualized in
Figures [22](#A6.F22 "Figure 22 ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It"),
[23](#A6.F23 "Figure 23 ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It"),

### E.7 Accuracy of Linear Probes

The results of the probing experiment, detailed in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Dissociation of Arithmetic Validation and Computation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It")
and
Appendix [D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Linear Probes ‣ Appendix D Experiment Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It"),
are presented for Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct,
and Phi-3-Mini-4k-Instruct in
Figure [20](#A6.F20 "Figure 20 ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It").
The findings indicate that for all models, near-perfect accuracy is
achieved by probes trained on the hidden representations of the residual
stream in the upper layers. Notably, Phi-3-Mini-4k-Instruct is the only
model that demonstrates significant probe accuracy in the middle layers.

### E.8 Residual Stream Patching

To bridge the gap between the models’ circuits responsible for
arithmetic computation and validation, we add the hidden representation
from higher layers—where the correct arithmetic result is linearly
encoded (see
Figure [20](#A6.F20 "Figure 20 ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It")—to
lower layers. Specifically, for Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct, we
intervene on layer 1 using the hidden representation from layer 22. For
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the intervention is performed on layer 2 using
the hidden representation from layer 16, while for
Phi-3-Mini-4k-Instruct, layer 1 is modified using the hidden
representation from layer 24. The results of these interventions are
depicted in
Figure [21](#A6.F21 "Figure 21 ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details ‣ The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It").

Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct, and
Phi-3-Mini-4k-Instruct exhibit significant improvements in accuracy
following these interventions. In contrast, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
demonstrates a more modest performance gain. We attribute this
difference to the simplicity of our approach and consider this a
promising direction for further investigation.

## Appendix F Implementation Details

For the majority of our circuit identification experiments, we used the
AutoCircuit library developed by [Miller et al. (2024)](#bib.bib24). For
the remaining experiments, we relied on the TransformerLens library
by [Nanda and Bloom (2022)](#bib.bib28). All models were loaded with
bfloat16 precision. The experiments were conducted on a single A100 GPU
with 80GB of memory, consuming approximately 350 GPU hours in total.
Additionally, GitHub Copilot was used as an assistant tool for parts of
the project’s source code development, and ChatGPT was used to correct
minor grammatical errors.
